name: The Chamber of True and False

lesson.title: The Algebra of True and False

sections.title: What Counts as a Proposition
sections.body:
A **proposition** is a declarative sentence that has exactly one truth value: it is either **true** or **false**, never both and never neither. Questions, commands and requests are not propositions, because there is nothing about them to be true or false.

An open sentence such as $x + 1 = 4$ is also not a proposition, because its truth value depends on a **free variable** you have not been told the value of. Fix the variable, or bind it with $\forall$ or $\exists$, and it becomes one.

The one operation you need before any table is **negation**. Written $\neg p$ and read *not $p$*, it is defined entirely by the fact that it **flips the truth value**: if $p$ is true then $\neg p$ is false, and if $p$ is false then $\neg p$ is true.
sections.code:
STATEMENT                                  A PROPOSITION?   TRUTH VALUE
-----------------------------------------  ---------------  -----------
"7 is a prime number."                     yes              T
"7 + 3 = 11."                              yes              F
"Every even integer above 2 is composite." yes              T
"What time is the lecture?"                no               -  a question
"Close the door."                          no               -  a command
"x + 1 = 4"                                no               -  depends on x
"This statement is false."                 no               -  self-referential

Negation flips the value and changes nothing else:
  p = "7 is a prime number."   is T,  so  ~p = "7 is not prime."     is F
  q = "7 + 3 = 11."            is F,  so  ~q = "7 + 3 is not 11."    is T

annotations.text: A proposition does not have to be true. 7 + 3 = 11 is false, and being definitely false is exactly what makes it a proposition.
A question has no truth value at all. Asking it is not asserting anything.
Free variable x. Say x = 3 and it becomes true; say x = 9 and it becomes false. Until you say, it is neither.
Negation is a one-input connective: it takes one truth value and returns the other one.

checkpoint.prompt: For each sentence, write `yes` if it is a proposition and `no` if it is not.
checkpoint.template:
"The number 12 is divisible by 5."       -> ___
"Add 3 to both sides."                   -> ___
"n is an odd number."                    -> ___
"Every prime greater than 2 is odd."     -> ___
checkpoint.explain: Being false does not disqualify a sentence: 12 is not divisible by 5, so the first sentence is a false proposition, which is still a proposition. The second is an instruction, so there is nothing in it to be true or false, and the third leaves $n$ free, so its truth value is not determined. The fourth pins everything down with *every*, so it asserts one definite thing - and it happens to be true.

sections.title: Conjunction, Disjunction, and the Truth Table
sections.body:
A **truth table** lists every possible assignment of truth values to the variables and computes the value of a compound proposition in each case. With $n$ distinct variables there are $2^n$ assignments, so the table has $2^n$ rows - two variables give four rows, three give eight.

**Conjunction** $p \land q$ is true only when $p$ and $q$ are both true. **Disjunction** $p \lor q$ is true when at least one of them is true, and this *or* is **inclusive**: $p \lor q$ is still true when both hold.

Because the table is exhaustive, it settles any question about a compound proposition by inspection rather than by argument. That is the whole reason propositional logic is tractable: the space of cases is finite and small.
sections.code:
p   q  |  ~p  |  p ^ q  |  p v q
-------+-----+---------+--------
T   T  |  F  |    T    |    T
T   F  |  F  |    F    |    T
F   T  |  T  |    F    |    T
F   F  |  T  |    F    |    F

Read down a column, not across a row: the column IS the connective.
  p ^ q  is T in exactly one row  - conjunction demands both
  p v q  is F in exactly one row  - inclusive or, still T when both hold

With n distinct variables the table has 2^n rows:
  n = 1 -> 2 rows,   n = 2 -> 4 rows,   n = 3 -> 8 rows.

annotations.text: Row order is a convention: count down in binary with T as 1. Keeping the same order every time makes two tables comparable at a glance.
The only row where p v q is false is the row where both are false. Everything else is true.
Inclusive or. English often means the exclusive one - tea or coffee - but mathematics never does unless it says so.
2^n grows fast, which is why hand tables stop being practical at around four variables.

checkpoint.prompt: Take $p$ to be true and $q$ to be false. Fill each blank with `T` or `F`.
checkpoint.explain: This is the second row of the standard table, evaluated one connective at a time. The conjunction fails because $q$ is false and conjunction needs *both*; the disjunction survives on $p$ alone, which is exactly the asymmetry between $\land$ and $\lor$. Negation simply reports the other value, so $\neg q$ is true precisely because $q$ is not.

sections.title: Implication, and Why False Implies Anything
sections.body:
The **implication** $p \Rightarrow q$ reads *if $p$ then $q$*; here $p$ is the **hypothesis** and $q$ the **conclusion**. It is defined to be false in exactly one row - the row where the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false - and true in the other three.

That is why $F \Rightarrow T$ and $F \Rightarrow F$ are both **true**. An implication is a promise about what happens *when the hypothesis holds*; if the hypothesis never holds, the promise was never triggered and so cannot have been broken. Such cases are called **vacuously true**.

Swapping and negating the two halves gives three relatives. The **converse** is $q \Rightarrow p$, the **inverse** is $\neg p \Rightarrow \neg q$, and the **contrapositive** is $\neg q \Rightarrow \neg p$. Only the contrapositive has the same truth table as the original.

The **biconditional** $p \Leftrightarrow q$ reads *$p$ if and only if $q$* and is true exactly when the two sides agree - it is the implication and its converse asserted together.
sections.code:
p   q  |  p -> q  |  ~p v q  |  q -> p  |  ~p -> ~q  |  ~q -> ~p  |  p <-> q
-------+----------+----------+----------+------------+------------+---------
T   T  |    T     |    T     |    T     |     T      |     T      |    T
T   F  |    F     |    F     |    T     |     T      |     F      |    F
F   T  |    T     |    T     |    F     |     F      |     T      |    F
F   F  |    T     |    T     |    T     |     T      |     T      |    T

Only a T hypothesis can ever make an implication F. Hence:
  F -> T is T    nothing was promised about a false hypothesis
  F -> F is T    the promise was never triggered, so it was never broken

Column (p -> q) matches column (~q -> ~p) exactly  -> the contrapositive.
Column (q -> p) matches column (~p -> ~q) exactly  -> converse and inverse
are equivalent to each other, and neither matches p -> q. Row 3 separates them.

annotations.text: The single F in the whole implication column: true hypothesis, false conclusion. Memorise this row and the rest follows.
Row 3 is F -> T, and it is true. It is also the row where the converse and the inverse part company with the original.
Vacuous truth is not a loophole - it is what makes 'every element of the empty set is purple' come out true.
Two identical columns is the definition of logical equivalence, so this line is already a complete proof that the contrapositive is equivalent.

checkpoint.prompt: Explain why $F \Rightarrow T$ is defined to be **true**, using the words *hypothesis* and *conclusion*, and say what would go wrong with the truth table if it were defined as false instead.
checkpoint.explain: An implication asserts only what happens when the hypothesis holds, so a false hypothesis leaves nothing to violate - there is no row in which the promise was made and then broken. If $F \Rightarrow T$ were false, then $\neg p \lor q$ would no longer match $p \Rightarrow q$, and a universally quantified claim such as *every prime above $2$ is odd* would be sunk by the even number $4$, which never satisfies the hypothesis in the first place.

sections.title: Tautology, Contradiction, and Equivalence
sections.body:
A compound proposition true in **every** row is a **tautology**, such as $p \lor 
eg p$. One false in every row is a **contradiction**, such as $p \land 
eg p$. Everything else is called contingent: its value depends on the row.

Two propositions are **logically equivalent**, written $P \equiv Q$, when their final columns are identical row for row. Equivalently, $P \equiv Q$ exactly when $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ is a tautology - so equivalence is a statement *about* formulas, while the biconditional is itself a formula.

**De Morgan's laws** are the two equivalences that push a negation through a connective, flipping it as they go: $$
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q \qquad 
eg(p \lor q) \equiv 
eg p \land 
eg q$$

Two more worth keeping: $p \Rightarrow q \equiv 
eg p \lor q$, and negating that with De Morgan gives $
eg(p \Rightarrow q) \equiv p \land 
eg q$ - the only way to break a promise is to meet the hypothesis and fail the conclusion.
sections.code:
De Morgan, checked row by row:

p   q  |  p ^ q  |  ~(p ^ q)  |  ~p v ~q  |  p v q  |  ~(p v q)  |  ~p ^ ~q
-------+---------+------------+-----------+---------+------------+---------
T   T  |    T    |     F      |     F     |    T    |     F      |    F
T   F  |    F    |     T      |     T     |    T    |     F      |    F
F   T  |    F    |     T      |     T     |    T    |     F      |    F
F   F  |    F    |     T      |     T     |    F    |     T      |    T

Columns 3 and 4 agree in every row  ->  ~(p ^ q) = ~p v ~q
Columns 6 and 7 agree in every row  ->  ~(p v q) = ~p ^ ~q

p v ~p   is T in every row   -> a tautology
p ^ ~p   is F in every row   -> a contradiction
Two formulas are logically equivalent exactly when their final columns match.

annotations.text: Row 1: p ^ q is T, so its negation is F, and ~p v ~q is F v F = F. They agree here and in the three rows below.
The bottom row is the only one where p v q is false, and the only one where ~p ^ ~q is true. That is why those two columns coincide.
Negation turned ^ into v. That swap is the whole content of De Morgan - dropping it is the most common algebra error in logic.
This is the working definition of equivalence: not 'they mean the same thing' but 'these two columns are the same column'.

checkpoint.prompt:
Put these steps into a valid order for verifying $
eg(p \lor q) \equiv 
eg p \land 
eg q$ by truth table.
fragments: Negate that column to obtain the column for $\neg(p \lor q)$.
List all four assignments of truth values to $p$ and $q$, one per row.
Combine those two columns into the column for $\neg p \land \neg q$.
Compute the column for $p \lor q$ in each row.
Observe that the two final columns agree in every row, so the formulas are logically equivalent.
Compute the columns for $\neg p$ and for $\neg q$.
checkpoint.explain: A truth table is built strictly inside-out: the rows must exist before any column can be filled, and a column for a compound can only be computed once every sub-formula it mentions already has one. The comparison is the last step and never the first, because equivalence is *concluded* from the completed columns rather than assumed while filling them.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the truth table for the implication $p \Rightarrow q$. Write `T` or `F` in each blank.
guided-practice.explain: Three of the four rows are true, which surprises everyone once. The single false row is the second, where the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails - that is the only shape a broken promise can take. The bottom two rows are vacuously true because their hypothesis is false, and that is precisely what makes $p \Rightarrow q$ agree with $\neg p \lor q$.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the truth table for the biconditional $p \Leftrightarrow q$. Write `T` or `F` in each blank.
guided-practice.explain: The biconditional is the *agreement* connective: true in the two rows where both sides carry the same value, false in the two where they differ. Note that it is true when both sides are **false**, which trips anyone reading it as *both hold*. It is exactly $(p \Rightarrow q) \land (q \Rightarrow p)$, so losing either direction loses the whole thing.

guided-practice.prompt: Evaluate $\neg(p \land \neg q) \lor r$ when $p$ is true, $q$ is false and $r$ is false. Give `T` or `F` at each step.

steps.label: value of NOT (p AND NOT q)

guided-practice.explain:
Evaluation follows the structure of the formula from the innermost sub-formula outwards, which is the same discipline as filling a truth table column by column. The single row you were handed is the one where the formula fails: $p$ true and $q$ false makes $p \land 
eg q$ true, its negation false, and with $r$ false the disjunction has nothing left to stand on. Note that $
eg(p \land 
eg q)$ is just $p \Rightarrow q$ in disguise.

guided-practice.prompt:
Give the truth value of each of these four implications, and justify each one by naming the truth value of its hypothesis and of its conclusion.

- (a) If $2 + 2 = 4$, then $3$ is prime.
- (b) If $2 + 2 = 4$, then $3$ is even.
- (c) If $2 + 2 = 5$, then $3$ is prime.
- (d) If $2 + 2 = 5$, then $3$ is even.
guided-practice.explain: Only (b) is false: its hypothesis $2 + 2 = 4$ is true and its conclusion *$3$ is even* is false, which is the one combination an implication forbids. (a) is true with both halves true, and (c) and (d) are **vacuously true** because $2 + 2 = 5$ is false, so no promise was ever triggered. Notice that the truth of (c) has nothing to do with any connection between arithmetic and primality - propositional logic sees only the two truth values, never the meaning.

guided-practice.prompt:
Prove that $
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q$ by constructing the full truth table. Show every row and every intermediate column, and state explicitly which feature of the finished table establishes the equivalence.
guided-practice.explain: With two variables the table has $2^2 = 4$ rows, so the proof is a **complete case analysis** - there is literally nothing left to check once the four rows are done, which is why a truth table is a proof and not merely evidence. Both columns come out $F, T, T, T$: the only row where $p \land q$ holds is the first, and that is exactly the only row where neither $\neg p$ nor $\neg q$ is available to satisfy the disjunction.

guided-practice.prompt: The converse of $p \Rightarrow q$ is $q \Rightarrow p$. Explain why an implication is **not** logically equivalent to its converse, name a row of the truth table where the two differ, and give a concrete English example of a true implication whose converse is false.
guided-practice.explain: The two columns disagree in two rows - $p$ true with $q$ false, and $p$ false with $q$ true - and one differing row is already enough to destroy an equivalence. *If $n$ is divisible by $4$ then $n$ is even* is true, while its converse fails at $n = 6$. Confusing a statement with its converse is the most common logical error in ordinary reasoning, and the contrapositive is the only one of the three relatives you may safely swap in.

guided-practice.prompt: Show by truth table that $p \Rightarrow q \equiv \neg p \lor q$. Then, using that equivalence together with De Morgan's laws, derive a form for $\neg(p \Rightarrow q)$ that uses no implication at all, and say in words what it means.
guided-practice.explain:
Both columns read $T, F, T, T$, so an implication is nothing more than a disjunction in costume - which is how implication gets eliminated in practice. Negating gives $
eg(
eg p \lor q) \equiv 
eg
eg p \land 
eg q \equiv p \land 
eg q$: to deny *if $p$ then $q$* you must exhibit a case where $p$ holds **and** $q$ fails. That is exactly the shape of a counterexample, and it is why disproving an implication never requires proving the opposite implication.

exam.prompt: Which of these is the definition of a **proposition**?
choices: Any sentence that contains at least one mathematical symbol.
A declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both.
A sentence whose truth value depends on the value of a free variable.
Any sentence that can be written using $\land$, $\lor$ and $\neg$.
exam.explain: The definition turns on having exactly one determinate truth value, not on notation and not on being true. *Not both* rules out self-referential sentences like *this statement is false*, and *either* rules out open sentences such as $x + 1 = 4$ - which is precisely what option 3 describes, and why option 3 is the trap.

exam.prompt: Which of these is the definition of a **tautology**?
choices: A compound proposition that is true in at least one row of its truth table.
A compound proposition that is false in every row of its truth table.
A compound proposition that is true in every row of its truth table.
Two compound propositions whose truth tables are identical.
exam.explain: *Every* row, not merely some row - a formula true in at least one row is only satisfiable, which is a far weaker property. Option 2 defines a contradiction and option 4 defines logical equivalence, and the three notions are linked: $P \equiv Q$ holds exactly when $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ is a tautology.

exam.prompt: Take $p$ true and $q$ false, and evaluate both sides of each De Morgan law. Write `T` or `F` in each blank.
exam.explain:
Each law's two sides land on the same value in this row, as they must in all four. Watch the connective flip rather than the values: $
eg p$ is false here, so the *disjunction* $
eg p \lor 
eg q$ still succeeds on $
eg q$ alone, while the *conjunction* $
eg p \land 
eg q$ is sunk by that same false $
eg p$.

exam.prompt: Evaluate $(p \lor q) \Rightarrow \neg r$ in the two rows shown. Write `T` or `F` in each blank.
exam.explain: The two rows share the *same* conclusion $\neg r = F$ yet give opposite results, which isolates the role of the hypothesis. In the first row the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails, giving the unique false pattern; in the second the hypothesis has collapsed to false, so the implication is vacuously true no matter what $\neg r$ does.

exam.prompt: Put these steps into a valid order for deciding, by truth table, whether a compound proposition is a tautology, a contradiction, or neither.
fragments: Build a column for each sub-formula, working from the innermost outwards.
Call it a tautology if that final column is $T$ in every row, a contradiction if it is $F$ in every row, and contingent otherwise.
Count the distinct variables in the formula; with $n$ of them the table needs $2^n$ rows.
Build the final column for the whole formula out of the sub-formula columns.
Write one row for each assignment of $T$ and $F$ to those variables.
exam.explain: The variable count comes first because it fixes the size of the table - $2^n$ rows - and everything after it is bookkeeping inside that fixed frame. Sub-formula columns must precede the final column, since a compound cannot be evaluated before its parts. The classification is then a single sweep down the finished column, and *contingent* is a real third answer rather than a failure to decide.

exam.prompt: Evaluate $\bigl((p \lor q) \land \neg r\bigr) \Rightarrow p$ when $p$ is false, $q$ is true and $r$ is false. Give `T` or `F` at each step.

steps.label: value of the hypothesis (p OR q) AND (NOT r)

exam.explain: This row assembles a **true** hypothesis on top of a **false** conclusion, which is the one and only way an implication can fail - so the formula is not a tautology, and a single row was enough to prove that. Note how $q$ carried the disjunction entirely on its own even though $p$ was false; refuting a claim about every row needs one row, while establishing it needs them all.

exam.prompt: Decide whether $\bigl((p \Rightarrow q) \land p\bigr) \Rightarrow q$ is a tautology, a contradiction, or neither. Build the truth table, state the value of the final column in each of the four rows, and justify your classification from it.
exam.explain: It is a tautology: the final column is $T$ in all four rows. The reason is structural rather than arithmetical - the hypothesis $(p \Rightarrow q) \land p$ can only hold in the top row, and in that row $q$ is true, so the forbidden pattern *true hypothesis, false conclusion* never arises. This tautology is the rule of inference called **modus ponens**, and its being a tautology is exactly what licenses detaching $q$ once you know both $p \Rightarrow q$ and $p$.

exam.prompt:
Prove that $p \Rightarrow q \equiv 
eg q \Rightarrow 
eg p$ using a truth table with columns for $
eg p$, $
eg q$, $p \Rightarrow q$ and $
eg q \Rightarrow 
eg p$. Then explain, citing a specific row, why the same argument does **not** work for the converse $q \Rightarrow p$.
exam.explain: Both columns read $T, F, T, T$, so the contrapositive is genuinely interchangeable with the original - which is what licenses proof by contrapositive later on. The converse column reads $T, T, F, T$ instead and parts company in the second and third rows; the row $p$ false, $q$ true is the cleanest witness, since $p \Rightarrow q$ is vacuously true there while $q \Rightarrow p$ has a true hypothesis and a false conclusion.

exam.prompt: Explain why $x + 1 = 4$ is not a proposition while $\exists x \in \mathbb{Z},\; x + 1 = 4$ is one, give the truth value of the second, and name what changed between the two sentences.
exam.explain: The first sentence has a **free variable**, so it has no single truth value - it is true at $x = 3$ and false everywhere else, and a proposition is not permitted to be both. The quantifier **binds** that variable, turning a family of claims into one claim about all of $\mathbb{Z}$, and that claim is true because $x = 3$ witnesses it. The gap between an open sentence and a proposition is the whole reason quantifiers exist.

exam.prompt:
Classify each of these as a tautology, a contradiction, or neither, and justify each answer from its truth table.

- (a) $(p \land \neg p) \Rightarrow q$
- (b) $p \land \neg p$
- (c) $p \Rightarrow p$
- (d) $p \Rightarrow \neg p$
exam.explain: (a) is a **tautology**: its hypothesis $p \land \neg p$ is false in every row, so the implication is vacuously true throughout - a contradiction really does imply everything. (b) is a contradiction and (c) is a tautology, since $p \Rightarrow p$ has matching halves in both of its rows. (d) is the interesting one: it is **neither**, because it is false when $p$ is true but true when $p$ is false, and being false somewhere is not the same as being false everywhere.

exam.prompt: Show by truth table that $p \Leftrightarrow q \equiv (p \Rightarrow q) \land (q \Rightarrow p)$. Then use the table to explain why knowing only that $p \Rightarrow q$ is true is not enough to conclude $p \Leftrightarrow q$, naming a row that makes the point.
exam.explain: Both columns read $T, F, F, T$, so a biconditional is precisely an implication conjoined with its converse - which is why *if and only if* proofs always have two halves. The row $p$ false, $q$ true settles the second part: there $p \Rightarrow q$ is vacuously true while $p \Leftrightarrow q$ is false, because the missing direction $q \Rightarrow p$ fails. One direction constrains the pair; only both directions force them to agree.
